I. The Basel Committee recognizes only Level 1 and Level 2 as regulatory categories; Level 3 provides examples and illustrations.

II. Because Level 3 is the most granular level, regulated banks must report their operational losses to the supervisor at Level 3.

III. Keeping the categories to the minimum meaningful number, and leaving finer detail to illustrative examples, helps protect the quality of risk information.

IV. The taxonomy was first defined after the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis, so conduct risk and cyber risk already appear in it as separate Level 1 event types.

options.D: I, III and IV only

Regulated financial services companies must report their operational risk to the regulator using this categorization.

question: An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing the coding of a closed loss event. Over six weeks, a corporate customer repeatedly drew on cheques deposited from an account at another bank before those funds had been collected. The investigation found that a branch operations officer had deliberately lifted the bank’s hold on the uncollected funds in exchange for kickbacks from the customer. The loss was SGD 2.4 million, and the event was coded as External Fraud, Theft and Fraud. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.A: Recode the event to Internal Fraud, Theft and Fraud, because the scheme involved at least one internal party.
options.B: Keep the event in External Fraud, Theft and Fraud, because check kiting is listed only under external fraud.
options.C: Recode the event to External Fraud, Systems Security, because the officer overrode a hold in the bank’s system.
options.D: Recode the event to Internal Fraud, Unauthorized Activity, because the officer acted outside his authority.

Stem summary: Singapore bank: customer draws on uncollected cheques with a bribed branch officer’s help; coded as External Fraud.

**Concept and theory**

The two fraud event types share almost the same definition and differ in one condition: who is involved.

| Level 1 type | GARP Table 3.1 definition |
|---|---|
| Internal Fraud | Losses due to acts of a type intended to defraud, misappropriate property or circumvent regulations, the law or company policy, excluding diversity/discrimination events, **which** **involves at least one internal party**. |
| External Fraud | Losses due to acts of a type intended to defraud, misappropriate property or circumvent the law, **by a third party**. |

Each Level 1 event type is split into Level 2 categories, twenty in all. I. In the concentric circle representation of an ORM framework created by ING in 2000, the loss database is the innermost circle and feeds the risk and control self-assessments (RCSAs) in the second circle.

II. In the same representation, key risk indicators (KRIs) form the outermost circle, where the firm draws lessons after large loss incidents or identified high-risk exposures.

III. Comprehensive, high-quality collection and analysis of loss data can reduce the occurrence and size of regulatory capital add-ons under Pillar 2.

Because the definition is about losses that have happened or could happen, knowing what has gone wrong in the past is the natural starting point for both managing and measuring it. question: The chief risk officer of a mid-sized Australian bank is reviewing the bank’s operational loss reporting threshold, currently set at AUD 5,000, after a board member questioned whether it is appropriate. Which statement about loss reporting thresholds is most accurate?

options.A: A zero reporting threshold is becoming the norm at large institutions, as it spares business units from estimating a loss before reporting.
options.B: The BCBS defines “material activities and exposures” and so requires every bank to apply a reporting threshold of exactly EUR 20,000.
options.C: The threshold chosen must be justified and must not suggest cherry-picking or capital manipulation; levels of 1,000 or 5,000 are common.

solution:
Stem summary: Chief risk officer of an Australian bank reviews the AUD 5,000 loss reporting threshold.

**Concept and theory**

A reporting threshold is the loss size below which incidents need not be recorded in the loss database. It exists because recording every tiny loss costs effort and adds little information, while setting it too high removes events that matter.

What the BCBS says: internal loss data must be comprehensive and capture “all material activities and exposures from all appropriate subsystems and geographic locations”. It does not define “material activities and exposures”. It sets a minimum collection threshold of EUR 20,000 (about USD 22,000).

question:
An operational risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing the internal loss record after an overnight batch job in the core banking system failed. Bank policy is to record any loss event whose gross amount is at least SGD 15,000. The analyst has identified the following items:

| Item | Description | Amount (SGD) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trading desk: trades left incomplete by the batch failure, closed out at a loss | 12,000 |
| 2 | Retail: compensation to online customers for the service interruption | 9,000 |
| 3 | Payments: late-payment charges paid to counterparties after the failure | 6,500 |
| 4 | Branch: ATM cash shortage on the same day, traced to a teller counting error | 3,000 |
| 5 | Insurance recovery received in respect of item 1 | 4,000 |

Which record is most consistent with best practice for operational loss data?

options.A: No record, because each item caused by the batch failure is individually below the SGD 15,000 threshold.
options.B: One grouped loss with gross loss SGD 23,500, no separate recovery, and net loss SGD 23,500.
options.C: One grouped loss with gross loss SGD 27,500, recovery SGD 4,000, and net loss SGD 23,500.
options.D: One grouped loss with gross loss SGD 30,500, recovery SGD 4,000, and net loss SGD 26,500.

question:
A senior risk analyst at a US asset manager is reviewing a closed internal fraud incident in which an employee diverted small amounts from a suspense account over a long period. The incident record shows the following dates:

| Field | Date |
|---|---|
| Date of occurrence | Monday 6 March 2023 |
| Date of discovery | Monday 15 September 2025 |
| Date of reporting | Thursday 18 September 2025 |
| Date of accounting (general ledger) | Wednesday 27 May 2026 |
| Action plan closed | Tuesday 30 June 2026 |

Which statement best describes what these dates show?

options.A: The three-day gap between discovery and reporting measures the visibility of issues in the firm, and shows the fraud was highly visible.
options.B: The gap of about 30 months between occurrence and discovery reflects poor visibility of issues, and such delays typically explain long lags to settlement.
options.C: The gap of about 30 months between occurrence and discovery reduced the eventual impact, because the loss built up slowly in thin slices.
options.D: Regulators require the date of accounting for internal reporting, so the incident belongs only to the firm’s internal loss figures for 2026.

solution:
Stem summary: US asset manager analyst interprets the four dates of a suspense-account fraud.

**Concept and theory**

Each operational incident has four important dates:

| Date | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Occurrence | When the event first happened |
| Discovery | When it was first identified |
| Reporting | When it entered the reporting database |
| Accounting (settlement) | When the financial impact entered the general ledger |

Regulators do not require a specific date type for internal reporting, but the gap between each pair of dates is informative:

- Occurrence to discovery reflects the visibility of issues in the organisation.
- Discovery to reporting shows how diligently incidents are reported to the risk function.

|---|---|---|
| 1 | Loss on a defaulted commercial loan, worsened because collateral was recorded incorrectly; the loss is accounted for in credit risk RWAs | 2.4 |

Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst applies boundary-event rules to four events to find the operational loss total.

question: A quantitative analyst at a Swiss asset manager is drafting a training note that compares operational risk data with market and credit risk data. Which statement is least accurate?

options.A: Operational risk data are specific to each firm and mostly unrelated to the behaviour of financial markets.
options.B: The frequency and impact distributions of operational risk data can have very wide tails.
options.C: Operational risk data are abundant, which makes them simpler to model than market and credit risk data.
options.D: Operational risk data can remain hidden for a long time, and their interpretation can be complex.

solution:
Stem summary: Swiss asset manager analyst identifies the least accurate statement about operational risk data features.

**Concept and theory**

Operational risk data differ from financial risk data in five ways, according to GARP:

1. They are specific to each firm and mostly unrelated to the behaviour of financial markets.
2. Their frequency and impact distributions can have very wide tails (extreme events).
3. They are scarce.
4. They can remain hidden for a long time.
5. Their interpretation can be complex, depending on the causes and downstream consequences.

These features have “profound consequences for the measurement and modelling of operational risk”: firm-specific, scarce, fat-tailed data are harder, not easier, to model than market prices or credit histories.

loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian credit union is preparing the risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) file for the payments unit. For the risk “fraudulent payment instruction executed”, the workshop recorded the two assessments below. Testing evidence confirms that the dual-authorisation control and the call-back verification control both operate effectively.

| Assessment | Basis of the assessment | Likelihood | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dual authorisation and call-back verification assumed absent | Likely | Major |
| 2 | Dual authorisation and call-back verification taken into account | Unlikely | Major |

Which of the following statements about these assessments is most accurate?

options.A: Assessment 1 is the residual risk, since it shows the exposure that would remain if the two controls were removed.
options.B: Assessment 1 is the inherent risk, and it also indicates the possible impact if the two key controls were to fail.
options.C: The gap between the two assessments signals that the controls are failing, so the risk must be escalated above appetite.
options.D: Only Assessment 2 belongs in the RCSA, since an RCSA evaluates risk after controls and never assesses it before them.

solution:
Stem summary: Credit union payments unit: two assessments of the same fraud risk, one assuming controls absent, one taking them into account.

**Concept and theory**

An RCSA asks a business unit to evaluate the likelihood and impact of its operational risks twice. The first pass ignores the existing controls and gives the **inherent risk**: the exposure the activity would carry if nothing stood in the way. The second pass takes the existing controls and their effectiveness into account and gives the **residual risk**: what is left after the controls do their work. The difference between the two is, in effect, the contribution of the controls.

Why assess both? The residual rating tells management whether the unit is within risk appetite today. The inherent rating answers a different quest […]

options.B: Customer impacts are commonly expressed as a percentage of the client base, which makes the definitions usable by units of very different sizes.

An impact scale is the severity axis of the RCSA. It turns a judgement such as “this would hurt us badly” into one of a small number of defined levels, so that different people in different units rate severity the same way. GARP describes four design features.

question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is recording likelihood ratings for the annual RCSA. The bank’s likelihood scale uses a one-year horizon:

| Rating | Probability of occurrence within one year |
|---|---|
| Remote | below 2.5% |
| Unlikely | 2.5% to below 10% |
| Possible | 10% to below 35% |
| Likely | 35% to below 60% |
| Highly likely | 60% or above |

The head of treasury operations describes a successful ransomware attack on the treasury platform as “roughly a 1-in-12-year event”. She adds that the platform is due to be replaced in three years and that such an attack would cost about AUD 45 million. Which probability and rating should the analyst record?

options.A: 8.3%, rated Unlikely
options.B: 2.1%, rated Remote
options.C: 23.0%, rated Possible
options.D: 64.8%, rated Highly likely

solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank treasury: convert a “1-in-12-year” ransomware estimate into a one-year probability and rating.

**Concept and theory**

A likelihood scale is the second axis of the RCSA. GARP says likelihood is expressed either as a percentage probability or as a frequency of occurrence (“once in $x$ years”). The two are linked by the RCSA’s time horizon, which is one year at most (sometimes a quarter or shorter). GARP is explicit that when risk managers speak of a 1-in-10-year event, they mean an event with a 10% chance of occurring within the next year, not once in a 10-year horizon. The scenario is a GBP 3.0 million loss in each unit.

| Unit | Annual revenue (GBP m) | Annual operating income (GBP m) |
|---|---|---|
| X: Private banking | 95 | 40 |
| Y: Retail banking | 1,900 | 750 |
| Group total | 4,600 | 1,200 |
